claims.text: Carbon doping during synthesis will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Carbon doping during synthesis will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
A Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-P-based alloy processed by rapid cooling can have marginal glass-forming ability and limited amorphous-phase thermal stability.
The intervention is incorporation of a precise, low concentration of a carbon-rich precursor into the melt or during processing.
Rapid quenching by methods such as melt spinning or laser ablation can provide a cooling rate high enough to capture the amorphous state.
Phosphorus addition supports amorphization and the formation of stable metallic-glass structures in high-entropy alloys.
Carbon doping may be less effective under slower cooling rates.
Carbon dopants will segregate to atomic interfaces or form nanoscale carbon-rich regions in the melt.
Interfacial segregation or nanoscale carbon-rich regions will mediate crystallite-nucleation kinetics.
Carbon dopants reduce atomic mobility.
Carbon dopants disrupt local atomic order and thereby hinder crystallite nucleation.
Carbon may form protective shells that stabilize the disordered structure.
The proposed carbon-induced changes increase the effective crystallization barrier and shift the thermal-stability window to higher temperatures.
Relative to an undoped alloy, carbon doping will produce a larger fully amorphous casting diameter.
Relative to an undoped alloy, carbon doping will produce a higher critical cooling rate as an indication of enhanced glass-forming ability.
Relative to an undoped alloy, carbon doping will increase the crystallization-onset temperature.
The beneficial effect exists only within an optimal carbon-concentration range.
Excess carbon may cause secondary-phase formation or embrittlement.
Too little carbon may be insufficient to impede nucleation.

Failure of carbon-doped samples to show statistically significant improvements in both glass-forming ability and crystallization-onset temperature relative to an identically processed undoped control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats both a higher critical cooling rate and a larger fully amorphous casting diameter as improvements in glass-forming ability. These metrics ordinarily vary in opposite directions with glass-forming ability, so the stated direction for critical cooling rate is inconsistent with the casting-diameter criterion.
